nameStory: The Rocky Aeolid gets its name from its preferred habitat among rocky tide pools and its membership in the aeolid group of sea slugs. 'Aeolid' comes from Aeolus, the Greek god of winds, perhaps referring to how these delicate creatures seem to dance with the ocean currents like leaves in the wind.
description: The Rocky Aeolid is a tiny sea slug that looks like a living jewel crawling through tide pools. This nudibranch (pronounced 'NEW-dih-brank,' meaning 'naked gills') is smaller than your pinky nail, typically reaching only about half an inch long. Its translucent body is adorned with finger-like projections called cerata that give it an almost coral-like appearance. These beautiful marine gastropods are shell-less snails that have evolved into some of the ocean's most colorful creatures.

idTips.label: Cerata arrangement
idTips.description: Multiple rows of finger-like projections extend from the back, feeling soft and jelly-like to gentle touch, arranged in distinct clusters that look like tiny sea anemone tentacles

idTips.label: Body translucency
idTips.description: The body appears glass-like or translucent white, allowing you to see internal structures as dark shadows beneath the surface

idTips.label: Rhinophores
idTips.description: Two club-shaped sensory tentacles at the head end that are often wrinkled or ridged, used for detecting chemical signals in the water

idTips.label: Size and movement
idTips.description: Typically less than 15mm long, moves with a smooth gliding motion across surfaces, leaving no visible slime trail

idTips.label: Oral tentacles
idTips.description: Two smooth tentacles near the mouth that are longer and more slender than the rhinophores, often actively feeling around surfaces

habitat: Rocky Aeolids live in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and under rocks from Maine to Connecticut. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found crawling on hydroids (their preferred food) attached to rock surfaces. Look for them in the lower intertidal zone where they're less likely to be exposed to air during low tide.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to warm, often found in shallow tide pools during April and May spawning season.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation time when warm water brings them into shallower areas, making them easier to spot during low tide exploration.
seasonality.fall: Still visible but less active as temperatures cool, often found deeper in crevices and under rocks.
seasonality.winter: Rarely observed due to cold water temperatures and rough seas, likely retreating to deeper, more protected waters.

funFact: Rocky Aeolids are solar-powered pirates — they steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own finger-like projections, essentially turning their prey's weapons into their own defense system!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small aeolid nudibranchs, but the Rocky Aeolid's translucent white body and clustered cerata arrangement help distinguish it. Memory trick: 'Rocky and white, clustered just right' — look for the pale coloration and grouped finger-like projections.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills' in Latin, referring to the exposed breathing structures on their backs. Don't confuse these marine sea slugs with terrestrial slugs found in gardens — they're completely different groups of animals that just happen to have similar body shapes.
compareHints: **Note: Limited reference material available for this species** Since this is the only Eubranchulus species documented in our New England dataset, compare it with other small aeolids in the family Eubranchidae by looking for the distinctive translucent white coloration and clustered cerata arrangement. Most other local aeolids tend to be more colorful or have different cerata patterns.
